transcript.heading: News Report One (American Male)
paras: Public libraries across the United States are expanding their services far beyond simply lending books, transforming into vibrant community hubs that offer a wide range of resources and programs for people of all ages. A new survey conducted by the American Library Association found that over 90 percent of public libraries now offer free access to computers and high-speed internet, critical services for people who cannot afford these at home. Many libraries have also added dedicated maker spaces equipped with 3D printers, sewing machines, and audio recording equipment, allowing community members to create projects they could not otherwise pursue. Additionally, libraries are increasingly offering free classes in digital literacy, resume writing, and English language instruction for immigrants. During tax season, many libraries provide free assistance with tax preparation for low-income residents. Library directors report that these expanded services have led to a 30 percent increase in visitor numbers over the past five years, demonstrating that public libraries remain essential institutions even in the digital age.

paras: Conservationists in Kenya are celebrating a significant victory in their efforts to protect endangered black rhinos, as new census data shows the population has increased by 15 percent over the past six years. The latest count, conducted using aerial surveys and ground patrols, estimates there are now over 900 black rhinos in the country, up from 780 in 2020. This positive trend is attributed to enhanced anti-poaching measures, including the deployment of specially trained rangers with advanced surveillance technology, as well as successful community engagement programs that give local residents a stake in wildlife conservation. The Kenyan government has also established new protected sanctuaries and implemented strict penalties for rhino poaching, which now carries a maximum sentence of life imprisonment. Despite this progress, conservationists caution that black rhinos remain critically endangered, with habitat loss and illegal wildlife trade continuing to pose serious threats. They emphasize that sustained funding and international cooperation will be necessary to ensure the long-term survival of the species.

transcript.heading: News Report Three (American Female)
paras: A new campaign launched by the European Union aims to cut food waste in half by 2030, as new figures reveal that approximately 88 million tons of food are wasted annually across EU member states, costing an estimated 143 billion euros. The campaign targets all stages of the food supply chain, from farms and food manufacturers to retailers and consumers. Farms are being encouraged to donate unsold produce to food banks rather than discarding it, while supermarkets are being urged to relax strict cosmetic standards for fruits and vegetables that often lead perfectly edible food to be thrown away simply because of unusual shapes or sizes. The EU is also calling on member states to improve date labeling practices, as research shows many consumers confuse "best before" dates with safety dates, leading them to discard food that is still perfectly safe to eat. For consumers, the campaign provides practical tips on meal planning, proper food storage, and using leftovers creatively. Officials say that reducing food waste would not only save money for households and businesses but also significantly reduce greenhouse gas emissions associated with food production and disposal.

When you add all that up, the Oak Street place might actually be a better deal. Also, it has in-unit laundry, which would save us a ton of time and money compared to using a laundromat.

Also, I read some reviews online saying the building can be noisy because there's a bar on the ground floor. Man: Hmm, that's a concern about the noise. I do need quiet when I'm working from home. What about parking? The Oak Street listing says there's assigned parking, but does it cost extra?

Woman: Let me check... Yes, parking is an additional $100 per month. But the Maple Avenue place doesn't come with parking at all—we'd have to find street parking, which can be really difficult in that area. We'd probably end up paying for a parking garage anyway, which would be at least that much.

Man: Right. Well, should we schedule viewings for both places so we can see them in person? Pictures can be misleading sometimes. I'd like to get a feel for the neighborhood and see how much natural light the apartments get.

Woman: That's a great idea. I'll also ask the landlords about their pet policies, just in case we decide to get a cat next year. And we should find out about the application process and what kind of fees we'll need to pay upfront.

transcript.heading: Passage One (British Female)
paras: Urban gardening, the practice of growing plants and food in cities, has been growing rapidly in popularity over the past decade, and for good reason. This green movement offers numerous benefits for individuals, communities, and the environment.

First and foremost, urban gardening provides access to fresh, nutritious produce for city dwellers. Many urban neighborhoods, particularly in low-income areas, are classified as "food deserts"—areas where residents have limited access to affordable fresh fruits and vegetables. Community gardens allow people to grow their own food, ensuring they have access to healthy produce at a fraction of the cost of buying it at grocery stores. Growing your own food also gives you control over what pesticides and fertilizers are used, allowing for organic, chemical-free produce.

Beyond the nutritional benefits, urban gardening has significant positive impacts on mental health and well-being. Research has shown that spending time in green spaces and engaging in gardening activities reduces stress, lowers anxiety levels, and improves overall mood. The physical activity involved in gardening—digging, planting, weeding, and harvesting—also provides moderate exercise, helping people stay active without the intensity of a formal workout. For older adults in particular, gardening offers a low-impact form of exercise that can improve mobility and flexibility while providing a sense of purpose.

Community gardens also serve as important social spaces that bring neighbors together. Working alongside other gardeners helps build social connections, reduces feelings of isolation, and creates a sense of community ownership and pride. Many community gardens host workshops, potlucks, and other events that strengthen neighborhood bonds and provide opportunities for people from diverse backgrounds to interact and share knowledge.

Environmentally, urban gardens help reduce the urban heat island effect by providing shade and cooling through evapotranspiration. Plants absorb carbon dioxide and release oxygen, improving air quality in polluted city environments. Gardens also help manage storm water runoff by absorbing rainwater, which reduces flooding and prevents pollutants from being washed into local waterways. Even small-scale container gardening on balconies and windowsills can contribute to these environmental benefits.

transcript.heading: Passage Two (American Male)
paras: Time management is one of the most critical skills for success in college and beyond, yet many students struggle to use their time effectively. The good news is that time management is not an innate talent— it's a skill that can be learned and improved with practice.

One of the most effective time management techniques is prioritization. Not all tasks are created equal, and it's important to distinguish between what is urgent and what is important. Urgent tasks demand immediate attention, while important tasks contribute to long-term goals and values. Many people fall into the trap of spending most of their time putting out fires—dealing with urgent tasks that may not be particularly important—while neglecting important but less urgent activities like studying for exams that are weeks away, exercising, or building relationships. The Eisenhower Matrix, a tool that categorizes tasks into four quadrants based on urgency and importance, can help students make better decisions about how to allocate their time.

Another common mistake is overcommitting. College offers so many opportunities—clubs, sports, social events, part-time jobs, internships—that it can be tempting to try to do everything. But taking on too many commitments leads to burnout and ensures that nothing gets your best effort. Learning to say no to activities that don't align with your priorities is essential. It's also helpful to plan your week in advance, setting aside specific blocks of time for studying, attending classes, exercising, socializing, and rest. Using a planner or calendar app to track deadlines and commitments can prevent last-minute cramming and forgotten assignments.

Procrastination is perhaps the biggest enemy of effective time management. Students often procrastinate on tasks they find difficult or unpleasant, choosing instead to engage in more enjoyable activities like scrolling through social media or watching videos. One effective strategy for overcoming procrastination is the "two-minute rule": if a task takes less than two minutes to complete, do it immediately rather than putting it off. For larger tasks, breaking them down into smaller, manageable steps makes them feel less overwhelming. For example, instead of thinking "write research paper," you could break it down into steps like "choose topic," "find three sources," "write introduction," and so on. The Pomodoro Technique—working for 25 minutes, then taking a 5-minute break—can also help maintain focus and prevent burnout during long study sessions.

transcript.heading: Passage Three (British Male)
paras: Animal-assisted therapy, often referred to as pet therapy, is a growing field that uses trained animals to help people improve their physical, emotional, and cognitive well-being. While dogs are the most commonly used therapy animals, cats, horses, birds, rabbits, and even dolphins can serve in therapeutic roles.

The use of animals for therapeutic purposes is not new. The ancient Greeks documented that horses seemed to have a calming effect on people with serious illnesses, and the first recorded use of animal-assisted therapy in a clinical setting occurred in the late 18th century at an English mental health institution, where patients were encouraged to interact with domestic animals as part of their treatment. However, it wasn't until the 1960s that animal-assisted therapy began to be formally studied and integrated into mainstream healthcare, largely due to the work of child psychologist Boris Levinson, who noticed that withdrawn children became more communicative when his dog was present during therapy sessions.

Today, animal-assisted therapy is used in a wide variety of settings, including hospitals, nursing homes, schools, mental health facilities, and rehabilitation centers. In hospitals, therapy dogs visit patients to help reduce anxiety and provide comfort, particularly for children undergoing painful medical procedures. Research has shown that interacting with therapy animals can lower blood pressure, reduce levels of stress hormones like cortisol, and even decrease the need for pain medication in some patients. In nursing homes, visits from therapy animals help combat loneliness and depression among residents, while also providing opportunities for gentle physical interaction like petting and grooming.

For children with autism spectrum disorder, animal-assisted therapy can help improve social skills and reduce anxiety. The non-judgmental presence of an animal can make children feel more comfortable communicating and interacting, and therapists often use animals as a bridge to help children connect with other people. In educational settings, therapy dogs are sometimes brought in to help children who struggle with reading—children often feel more comfortable reading aloud to a dog, which doesn't judge them if they make mistakes, helping to build confidence and fluency.

It's important to note that therapy animals go through extensive training and certification to ensure they are well-behaved, calm, and comfortable in various environments. Their handlers also receive training to work effectively with different populations. While animal-assisted therapy is not a cure for any condition, numerous studies have documented its benefits as a complementary treatment that can improve quality of life for many people.
